author: Claude (English teacher role), drafted directly (Gemini quota exhausted for this session)
basis: New mission, no workbook source; written per docs/plans/new-mission-playbook.md, angle distinct from sdg1 (general safety-net framing) and sdg1-2 (labor-market framing): social mobility and scholarships specifically. Facts and sources: NTU economics department study using national tax records for the 1993-1995 birth cohort found a child from a rich household is about six times more likely to be admitted to NTU than a child from a poor household; NTU/public-university students' median household income (NTU >NT$1.5M, other public universities >NT$1M) far above the overall sample median (~NT$860,000), producing a 'reverse redistribution' effect since elite public universities receive more government funding per student (報導者/The Reporter coverage of the NTU study, also covered by 商業周刊/今周刊). Stars Program (繁星計畫): multi-track admission by in-school standing rather than only national exam score, designed to widen access for rural/under-resourced students. Ministry of Education's University System Financial Aid Program for Disadvantaged Students (大專校院不利處境學生助學計畫), since the 2007 academic year, targets households in the bottom 40% of income distribution with four kinds of support: tuition subsidy, living stipend, emergency relief, housing subsidy (教育部圓夢助學網/coloan.moe.gov.tw). Early-intervention argument sourced to 獨立評論 commentary on rural education and poverty. Cram-school spending advantage and post-admission cost burden stated in general terms, not invented as precise figures.

slides.1: Admission data reveal an uncomfortable pattern. A student from a wealthy household is roughly six times more likely to be admitted to Taiwan's most prestigious university than one from a poor household.
slides.2: SDG 1 targets poverty in every form, and this talk interrogates the mechanism most often credited with solving it: education. Does schooling genuinely interrupt the cycle that transmits poverty across generations, or does it just relabel it?
slides.3: The admissions data are stark. Students at Taiwan's most prestigious university typically come from households earning upward of NT$1.5 million a year, well above the national median of roughly NT$860,000.
slides.4: Wealthier households invest heavily in private tutoring, which quietly shapes how well a child performs on the entrance exams that decide admission. Households without that budget cannot buy the same head start.
slides.5: Here lies a genuine puzzle: Taiwan's most prestigious public universities receive much more government funding per student. Yet their enrollment skews toward wealthier households rather than poorer ones, meaning a system designed to equalize things ends up doing the opposite.
slides.6: Admission alone does not remove the burden facing a low-income student. They still absorb tuition, textbooks, and rent, while every hour spent studying is an hour not spent earning an income.
slides.7: Genuine progress clearly exists here. Taiwan has established the Stars Program, an admissions track that evaluates students by their standing within their own school rather than by a single national exam.
slides.8: Since 2007, Taiwan has run a broader assistance program. It provides tuition subsidies, living stipends, emergency relief, and housing help specifically to students from the poorest forty percent of households.
slides.9: Financial aid alone rarely solves the whole underlying problem completely. What actually helps most is pairing a scholarship with mentorship, because guidance is valued as much as the money itself.
slides.10: One evident solution involves allocating aid according to financial need rather than exam performance alone. This ensures support reaches those who genuinely require it, not merely those who already tested well.
slides.11: Money alone cannot solve this. Instead of distributing funds in isolation, institutions could pair every scholarship with a dedicated mentor, someone who guides a student rather than simply subsidizing them.
slides.12: By the time a student reaches university, meaningful intervention already arrives too late. Support ought to begin far earlier, ideally before kindergarten, since the gap separating rich and poor compounds with each passing year.
slides.13: If financial aid and mentorship reach a student early enough, that student can complete a degree. This can meaningfully alter the trajectory of an entire family, not merely their own prospects.
slides.14: However, a degree does not automatically erase every disadvantage. It cannot pay off inherited family debt, and a wealthier graduate still enters the job market with a far larger network and more financial support.
slides.15: However, the entrance exam continues to reward precisely what wealthier families can purchase: years of paid tutoring. That edge allows the same cycle to persist quietly into the next generation as well.
slides.16: However, a more promising path clearly exists here: programs combining funding with steady mentorship show the strongest outcomes. It is mentorship that ultimately breaks the entire cycle, not money alone.
slides.17: So what does the evidence actually reveal? Wealthier students still gain admission more easily, although the Stars Program and government aid schemes are clearly helping poorer students close that gap.
slides.18: This matters inside this very lecture hall today. Someone sitting beside you may already depend entirely on precisely this exact scholarship, which makes the story anything but distant or abstract.
slides.19: So here is a concrete step you can take today. Volunteer to tutor a younger student, or actively advocate for your institution to attach mentorship to every scholarship it awards.
slides.20: Education ought to open an identical door for every single student, irrespective of family income. Taiwan has merely begun that work, and completing it will fall entirely to your generation.
